SCIENCE IN EXILE
BY
Dr. Annemarie Clark-Schwarzenbach
At Istanbul, in the autumn of 1933, I found my
distinguished compatriot, Professor Malche of Switzerland,
hard at work on the task of reorganizing that ancient and
venerable seat of learning, the University of Istanbul, –
no sinecure, for it meant the breaking up of a long-established
system of teaching – a very Babylonian Tower reared up on a
mass of dogmatic commentaries and topped by the Koran. "Pro¬
fessors" by the hundred kept adding their individual "bricks"
to this edifice, while the brain of thousands of students
were put to doing nothing better than parroting commentaries,
maxims and prayers. Then required to prepare a thesis, they
would employ the simple expedient of translating some foreign
work, most often French. They had not even a rudimentary con¬
ception of how to put their minds to any constructive use.
Professor Malche began the weeding-out process by
getting rid of much dead wood. He eliminated a considerable
number of superannuated Mohamedan teachers and replaced them
with German professors who had become available at that time.
Many distinguishednen. Scholars had joined the exodus from
Germany, swept out of their country by the hug tidal wavel
of Hitlerism. More than thirty refugees accepted his call,
among them scientists of world renown, such as the philosopher
Reichenbach, and Nissen, the medical authority, assistant
to that great surgeon, Sauerbruch.1)
Turkey, for a long time dubbed "the sick Man on the
Bosporus," by the political imperialists, had wrenched itself
free from the "protection" of foreign powers. So it was per¬
haps not by mere accident, but rather symbolic of the irony
of history, that in its march towards achievement of national
emancipation and social as well as economic independence and
process, the young Turkish Republic should turn towards the
liberal spirit of the West at a moment when Germany, till
now so et preeminently the home of the highest expression of European
culture, held that it wished to do without it. In Hitler's
Germany one had begun to grade scholars and scientists not
according to their spiritual statue, but rather by their
attitude towards the National-Socialist Totalitarian State.
These men who found themselves unable to make obeisance to
this dogma, found new fields of activity in Turkey, an "oriental"
land.
In Bagdad I learned that the head of the local
Jewish Hospital – that city's best medical institution – was a
German émigré doctor, formerly a distinguished member of the
staff of the Virchow-Hospital in Berlin [ev. Bekannter von Maria Daelen?]. Just then he was

occupied in supervising the installation of an X-Bay Room.
The year following, at Teheran, I met Professor Haas, of
the Hochschule für Politik (College of Political science)
in Berlin, another German émigré. Confronted by problems
similar to those encounterd by the Turkish Republic, the
Iranian Government, which was facing developments not unlike
those in Turkey, had called in Professor Haas to serve as
adviser in matters of science and education. Also in Persia,
at about the same epoch there was another case that came to
my notice: Professor Herzfeld, the most famous among German
archeologists, was being forced to leave Persepolis, the
discovery and exploration of which had been his achievement
and where excavations had been made for years under his direction.
He was deprived of his chair at the University in the new
Berlin of Hitler. He went to America, where, subsequently,
he found a new sphere of activity at the Institute for Ad¬
vanced Study at Princeton. One of his ablest ossistants at
Persepolis, a young German architect of partly Jewish extraction,
some six months later committed guide at Isfahan in his
desperation at being forbidden to work in his Fatherland.
It may, perhaps, be wrong to cite individual cases,
no matter how urgent their human appeal, when wholesale in¬
justice is claiming victims by the thousand. But how could
one avoid mentioning the case of that great writer and Nobel
Prize Winner Thomas Mann, known to the world of civilization
as the personification of all that is best and purest in
German literature and German altruism? When the Hitler Government
recently deprived him of his citzenship, this was felt as a
profound shock by a very large number of people, regardless of
the color of their politics.
So as to clear up the erroneous notion held by so many
well-meaning but deluded persons, namely, that only Jews, commu¬
nists, pacifists, and other "subversive elements" quit Germany
voluntarily, or by compulsion, it might be helpful to submit
some statistical data regarding the scientists thus driven into
exile, and to mention the number of Nobel Prize Winners who
were forced to emigrate. "Science in Exile" is but a part of
the tremendous problem of this mass emigration from Germany
that the world must face. History has known other tragic
instances of mass migrations, which have redounded to the advantage
of the countries that have offered their hospitality to the
emigrants; one needs only to recall the Portuguese Jews in
Holland, or the French Huguenots in Prussie, who at best became
amalgamated and assimilated with their host people. They could
never have played a fruitful or active part in the struggle that
drove them from their homeland. Maas emigration is necessarily
tragic, especially when based upon purely nationalistic causes
and a consequence of deep-seated antagonisms. The emigrant's
fate is ever a tragic one so long as he persists in considering
himself an exile in a host country and longingly yearns for the
bour of his return to the fatherland – an hour that never comes,
for even if a new revolution may open the way back to the
home country, there have been developments that have come
about in their absence and without their cooperation, which
make them feel ill at case and as mere "guests in their home-
land."
German emigration under the Hitler regime is better
off in that respect, because what is taking place in Germany
today is not a national and a German conflict, but the great
showdown faced by the whole world between dictatorship and
democracy. The struggle in Spain proves that the battle
fronts no longer are drawn along vertical national frontiers,
but that the lines of demarcation run horizontally and are
defined by Fascism and Anti-Fascism.
To call the group of scholars and scientists swept
along on the tide of anti-Fascist emigration a group of "exiles"
would be less than apt. Nowhere could science ever be in exile.
At least not in this day and age. For the discoveries of Albert
Einstein were less a German than a univeral achievement. Science
and especially mathematics and the natural sciences, – long
before the World War had ceased to be hemmed in by national
boundaries. The scientists and explorers of all lands were in
vital and close touch with one another. The mathematicians in
America kept abreast and were well aware of the progress
attained by their collegues in the universities of Germany.
The preeminence of the science of mathematics in this inter¬
national scientific exchange is simply due to the fact that
here the problem of language is less of an obstacle. Mathemati¬
cal theorems are expressed by formulae of universal validity
and thus may be internationally understood.
The soil that nurtures science is of spiritual nature,
entirely apart from the "blood and soil" adopted by the Nazis
as the degraded symbols of a degraded and sinister cult, fostered
by them to breed low instincts and prejudice; never, from the
dawn of history, has the progress of science been confined within
[*or political]
geographical [* added above line] boundaries – it has ever been the heritage of
those people who dwelt in peace and freedom and thus possessed
leisure and an open spirit, without which the arts and sciences
can never flourish.
Those German émigrés – doctor, writers, and others
who sought asylum in Russia, did so, almost without exception,
because of their political convictions, while the great number
of scientists of all kinds who turned to the United States each
went seperately, impelled by a great variety of personal motives.
As to them it may be said that with us Europeans it has ever
been a tradition, more true today than ever, to look upon
America as the land of the future – a receptive, a consecrated
land, the home par excellence of the pioneer spirit. To many
it has meant a promise fulfilled: just to mention a few of
the more distinguished names –
Professor James Franck is now lecturing at Johns Hopkins
University in Baltmore; Professors Friedländer, Courant,
Lehman, and Hartleben are lecturing at New York University;
Professor Köhler occupies a chair at Swarthmore; Professor
Geiger teaches at Vassar College, while Professor Tillich, who
as a theologian and member of the socialist Party in Germany
must have felt a rank outsider in the Fatherland, now finds that
in America it is not thought to be shocking for a Christian
theologian to belong to a Leftist movement in politics.
At the New School for social Research the "University
in Exile" has been incorporated into the Faculty and consists
of sixteen German professors, among them the psychologist
Wertheimer, the distinguished jurist Simons, and others.
This type of institution, however, should perhaps be character¬
ized as a mere stopgap, for the German scholars who are making
their contribution to the development of science in America,
should not do so as a group of foreigners, but should, each in
his own sphere, arrive to make it his high mission to fullill
his task to the utmost of his ability.
Prince Loewenstein is successfully occupied in
greating a "German Akademie" in America, whose purpose it shall
be to serve as a centre for the cultivation and preservation
of the German language, so as to save it from the doom of ex¬
tinction – a natural consequence of emigration and one of its
greatest problems. whether this will provide a method of
accomplishing this purpose remains to be seen. There is
to be another aspect – a practical one – to this undertaking:
the German "Akademie" is to arrange lectures, courses, and
will provide a prize – not for the exiled author most in need
of a stipend, but for the winter who produces the best book
written in the German language.
The most felicitous example of a solution of the
problem of the exile is to be found at the Institute for Ad¬
venced Study at Princeton. It was inaugerated in the spring
of 1933. It's Director, Dr. Abraham Flexner, thus desired to
provide an opportunity for scientists and advanced students
to freely pursue their scientifie studies unhampered by the
various limitations and restrictions ordinary placed upon
students at colleges and universities. Though this idea had
already been evolved a few years previously, independent of
the catastrophe that had overtaken German science and culture,
from the spring of 1933 both parties stood to profit by it:
the emigrants from the German universities, and the Institute.
At the "School of the humanities" Professor Herzfeld and the
archeologist Panofsky from Hamburg are teaching, while Albert
Einstein occupies a chair at the School of Mathmatics, as
do also Professor Hermann Weyl of the University of Göttingen,
and Professors Vehlen, von Neumann, Alexander and Mosse.
Einstein has stated that to him the call to Princeton meant
"to be exiled into Paradise."
Over the portal of the great hall of the University
of Heidelberg this beautiful description used to be found:
"To the Living Spirit." This was changed, on the occasion of
the recent celebration of Heidelberg's 550th anniversary, and
now reads: "To the German Spirit." Science in the Occident
evolved and grew out of that "Living Spirit" which can only
flourish where there is peace and freedom, and which patiently
seeks and delves after knowledge and truth. So, while banished
from Germany and homeless in Europe, driven out by bitter
struggle and strife, at Princeton it testifies to the fact
that America has reached mature spiritual stature and is now
ready to become the custodian of humanity's most precious
treasure. [vertical space]
